subject: Mathematics
central_question: How can relations and functions be classified, combined and inverted using precise set-theoretic conditions?
in_scope_units: 1.1 Introduction: relations as subsets of Cartesian products and functions as special relations.
1.2 Types of Relations: reflexive, symmetric, transitive and equivalence relations.
1.3 Types of Functions: one-one, many-one, into, onto and bijective functions.
1.4 Composition of Functions and Invertible Function: composition, identity maps and inverse functions.
1.5 Binary Operations: closure and binary operations on a set.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every symmetric relation is an equivalence relation.
known_pitfalls.correction: An equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

known_pitfalls.claim: A one-one function is automatically onto.
known_pitfalls.correction: One-one and onto are independent in general; on a finite set X, a map X to X that is one-one is onto.

known_pitfalls.claim: If f and g are invertible, then the inverse of g o f is g inverse o f inverse.
known_pitfalls.correction: The order reverses: (g o f)^(-1) = f^(-1) o g^(-1).

known_pitfalls.claim: Any rule on A x A is a binary operation on A.
known_pitfalls.correction: The output must belong to A for every ordered pair in A x A.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Example 5 to verify that divisibility of a-b by 2 defines an equivalence relation on integers.
Use NCERT Exercise 1.2 Question 7(i) to classify f(x)=3-4x as one-one and onto.
Use the NCERT composition example with f(x)=4x+3 to obtain and verify the inverse.
Use NCERT Exercise 1.4 questions to test whether a stated rule is a binary operation.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter contains Exercises 1.1 to 1.4 followed by the Miscellaneous Exercise on Chapter 1.
